headline: High: shared filesystem and MCP-backed tooling create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict risks; compliance gaps are also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can read/write workflow artifacts and Agent B ingests files, AGENTS.md, README.md, and runtime-injected MCP/hooks. That creates a plausible path for A-produced content to steer B’s tool use, even though no direct pairwise exploit is documented. B’s permissive tool surface makes the interaction more concerning than manual copy-paste.
conditions: IF Agent A writes attacker-controlled instructions into shared artifacts that Agent B later reads
IF Agent B treats repository or workspace text as trusted tool directives
mitigations: Restrict B to a read-only view of A outputs
Add provenance tags to A-generated files
Disable automatic instruction-following from workspace text
Review MCP hook inputs before execution
requires-engineering: add content-safety filtering between A and B

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches artifacts and parameters with allowlisted egress, while B touches project code, session history, and provider auth prompts with broad egress. If they share a workspace or installation, B can expose A-originated sensitive artifacts to external services. The profiles do not prove a shared directory, so this is inferred and kept at medium.
conditions: IF A and B operate on the same workspace or installation
IF B uploads or transmits files from that workspace to external APIs
mitigations: Separate A and B into distinct workspaces
Remove secrets from shared project files
Disable B uploads for sensitive directories
Rotate any credentials present in shared files
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has API access and workflow execution context; B has broad network egress, subprocesses, browser access, and multiple-instance support. Their write-like effects can overlap on shared project state or external services, but the profiles do not show unrestricted same-directory filesystem writes or git locking, so the conflict is plausible rather than proven.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same project state or external resource
IF no orchestrator lock serializes their writes
mitigations: Serialize writes through one orchestrator
Assign disjoint resource scopes
Pause B while A mutates shared state
Check for stale state before commits or API writes
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces workflow outputs and B has messaging, task creation, and browser/tooling that can act on upstream content. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles suggest this pathway but do not document a direct automation chain, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF B consumes A output without verification
IF B uses that output to create tasks, messages, or external actions
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A output
Add validation checks on A-produced artifacts
Limit B to read-only summarization of A results
Log provenance for every downstream action
requires-engineering: insert a verification gate between agents

E_compliance.rationale: A is an open-source workflow engine with allowlisted egress, while B handles provider auth prompts, telemetry, and project code under broad egress. That combination raises retention and residency mismatch risk if regulated data flows through B, but the profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction or certification conflict. Uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through B’s telemetry or external APIs
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the shared project data
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from B inputs
Review telemetry settings before use
Document retention for shared artifacts
Use separate environments for regulated workloads
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
